title: Graceful capacity attenuation for dedicated rollouts
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem:
When performing dedicated GPU pool upgrades we frequently observe short-lived capacity shocks as nodes are cordoned and KVs/weights are migrated. Existing drain workflows try to preserve headroom by evicting whole slots or tenant slices, but in mixed-tenant pools this leads to step changes in available concurrency and transient SLA degradation for latency-sensitive tenants.

Goal:
Implement a controller and rollout strategy that attenuates capacity reduction during upgrades with fine-grained, time-smoothed admission controls and an autoscaler handshake so the fleet experiences a controlled ramp-down instead of abrupt drops. The controller should integrate with rollout gates (LTS channels), respect tenant QoS reservations, and provide observability hooks for per-tenant admission curves and predicted SLO impact.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Deceleration windows: introduce the concept of a deceleration window for each upgrade wave. Instead of immediately marking capacity as unavailable, mark slices with a progressive attenuation factor (0.0-1.0) that reduces accepted concurrency over a configurable window (e.g., 5-30 minutes).
2) Slope-limited admission: implement slope-limiting on per-tenant admission controllers so accepted QPS/token concurrency follows a bounded derivative (max change per minute). This prevents stepwise eviction effects when multiple pods are drained in close succession.
3) Autoscaler handshake API: extend the autoscaler contract with an API that allows the rollout controller to request temporary headroom target adjustments and informs the autoscaler of planned attenuation so it can pre-warm or delay scaling decisions.
4) Tenant ramp profiles: allow tenants with explicit QoS reservations to register ramp profiles (fast, standard, conservative) that the controller uses to shape attenuation. Non-reserved tenants fall back to cluster defaults.
5) Predictive SLO impact modeling: before applying a deceleration window, run a short simulation using recent per-tenant latency percentiles and concurrency curves to estimate expected 95th-percentile latency delta. If predicted delta exceeds a threshold, require an additional rollout gate approval.
6) Observability and gating: emit per-wave metrics (attenuation fraction over time, predicted vs actual SLO delta, autoscaler handshake events) and surface them in the Console rollout page with a small-signal preview graph.

Design details and APIs:
- AttenuationUnit: (string identifier) attached to pool slices; state contains target_fraction (string, e.g., "0.7"), window_start, window_duration. Controller computes live admission multiplier = smoothstep from 1.0 to target_fraction over window_duration.
- Handshake endpoints: /autoscaler/attenuation-request and /autoscaler/attenuation-status (internal service-to-service calls, authenticated via mTLS). Request includes pool_id, wave_id, requested_headroom_delta, expected_window_sec. Response contains autoscaler_consent: true/false and recommended_prewarm_minutes.
- Rollout policy flags: allow config on LTS channel or per-release: allow_deceleration=true/false, max_slope_per_minute=0.05, max_predicted_slo_delta_p95_ms=50.

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit + integration tests for slope-limiter and attenuation multiplier logic.
- End-to-end simulation harness that can replay production traces and verify the same upgrade applied with attenuation yields lower 95th latency spikes compared to current hard-evict path.
- Autoscaler handshake implemented and exercised in CI with a mock autoscaler returning consent and prewarm guidance.
- Console rollout UI shows attenuation preview and historical comparison for at least one internal canary rollout.
- Rollout policy default is conservative and must be explicitly enabled on LTS channels before use.

Telemetry & SLOs to monitor during canary:
- Per-tenant p95 latency delta (baseline vs during wave) reported every minute.
- Attenuation adherence: actual admission fraction vs target fraction.
- Autoscaler latency: time between attenuation request and autoscaler consent or denial.
- Incidents: any tenant with p95 delta > 80ms is an automatic pause of the wave.

Risk and mitigation:
- Risk: Autoscaler may not respect requested headroom leading to unexpected capacity crunch. Mitigation: conservative defaults and prewarm recommendations; add auto-fallback to immediate rollback if autoscaler denies consent and predicted SLO delta is high.
- Risk: Complexity of new admission path introduces bugs that bypass tenant reservations. Mitigation: explicit tests and a feature-flag gating plus phased internal canary rollout.
- Risk: Increased rollout latency (upgrades take longer). Mitigation: tradeoff accepted for higher SLA stability; provide operators an "expedite" flag to bypass attenuation for critical security patches with human approval.

Migration plan:
- Phase 0 (experimentation): implement controller behind feature flag; run synthetic canaries on staging pools with production trace replay.
- Phase 1 (internal canary): enable on non-customer-facing dedicated pools; monitor telemetry for 2 weeks.
- Phase 2 (selected customers): opt-in per-customer on Dedicated with documented ramp profiles.
- Phase 3 (default LTS): flip default for new patch releases once metrics are within thresholds.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/design/deceleration-controller-v1
- Simulation harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rollout-sim
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5581

Notes on uniqueness vs existing upgrades work:
This ticket introduces time-smoothed attenuation and an autoscaler handshake; unlike prior work focused on discrete evacuation and buffer slices, the focus here is continuous admission shaping with tenant ramp profiles and predictive SLO checks. It complements existing drain orchestration but aims to reduce delta-induced latency spikes by controlling the rate of capacity reduction rather than the magnitude alone.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Controller branch merged behind feature-flag and unit-tested.
2) Integration tests confirm slope-limiter behavior across boundary conditions.
3) Simulation shows >=30% reduction in p95 spike magnitude for staged canaries.
4) Autoscaler handshake exercised in CI and logs recorded in Console.
5) Rollout UI displays attenuation preview for the internal canary wave.
updates: 2025-01-15: RFC posted to #release-eng; initial feedback from infra SRE suggests adding prewarm window to handshake.
2025-01-22: Spike completed — prototype slope-limiter implemented in admission layer (branch: feature/attenuation-slope). Observed smoother p95 curve in sim replay.
2025-01-30: Drafted autoscaler handshake contract and shared with autoscaler owners. They requested explicit recommended_prewarm_minutes field.
2025-02-05: PR 5581 opened for controller core and mock autoscaler. Running CI integration tests against sim harness.
2025-02-08: Canaries scheduled for next internal wave (2025-02-12). Monitoring dashboards prepared.
next_steps: Run internal canary, collect telemetry for 10 days, iterate on default slope and max_predicted_slo_delta thresholds.
